messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Malia was 46 when she first came to treatment, a married musician who had built her life around performance, rehearsal, and the small rituals that kept her days orderly. Before the illness, she had been known for her reliability: she arrived early to gigs, kept her instruments and scores meticulously arranged, and moved through her work with the confidence of someone used to breathing deeply before a phrase and trusting her body to do what it had always done. That sense of bodily certainty changed abruptly when she became seriously ill in a way that made breathing itself feel precarious. She described a period in which shortness of breath was no longer an occasional discomfort but a terrifying sign that something was very wrong, and the memory of those days remained vivid in the way she still spoke about “not getting enough air” as if she were back in the middle of it.

What stayed with her most from the illness was the sequence of examinations and procedures around it. She could still recall the antiseptic smell of medical rooms, the sharpness of disinfectant and latex, and the particular atmosphere of a hospital corridor that seemed to signal danger before anyone had said a word. Even now, those smells could pull her back instantly. A whiff of cleaning solution in a public building, or the scent attached to a clinic waiting room, made her stomach drop and her chest tighten before she had time to tell herself she was safe. The same happened when she had to undergo a medical examination or procedure. She would become tense before anyone touched her, her whole body bracing as though she were about to lose control again. She said that in those moments she was less afraid of pain than of what her body might do, and she had come to believe that medical settings were places where she had little power to protect herself.

Over time, Malia began arranging her life around the few places where she felt safe. She and her husband still lived in the same home, but she moved through it like someone checking the boundaries of a narrow refuge. At night she often woke suddenly, alert and scanning the room, needing to check whether she was safe before she could settle back to sleep. She described these awakenings without drama, but with a weariness that suggested they had become part of her nightly routine. She also noticed that her body would react before she had formed a clear thought about danger: a sudden rush of alarm, a tightening in her chest, a startle response to a smell or a bodily sensation that seemed to arrive in advance of reason. Because of this, she found herself relying on only a very limited number of places where she could relax. Her own home, and a few carefully chosen familiar rooms, felt tolerable; elsewhere she remained on edge, aware that she might have to leave if her body gave her a signal she could not control.

These changes reached into her work as well. As a musician, Malia had once moved easily between rehearsal spaces, performance venues, and the practical demands of travel. After the illness, she began avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever she could, and that avoidance shaped how she handled ordinary life. She delayed appointments, found excuses not to attend checkups, and felt a surge of dread if a venue was near a medical center or if a car siren sounded in the distance on the way to work. She had started to pass through her professional world with more caution, sometimes declining opportunities that would have required unfamiliar places or close contact with medical settings. The consequences accumulated quietly: more dependence on her husband for errands she once would have done without thought, more time spent rehearsing only in spaces she already knew, more cancellations than she liked to admit.

In private, Malia’s thoughts turned harshly inward. She would imagine how life might have been different if the illness had not happened, returning again and again to the lost version of herself who had not become so fearful and constrained. She told herself that she deserved to suffer because of what had happened, as if enduring anxiety and bodily fear were a fitting punishment. At the same time, she doubted her own judgment. She worried that she could not trust herself to do the right thing if another medical crisis came up, and that self-doubt made even straightforward decisions feel loaded. She called herself inadequate and, with painful regularity, interpreted her reactions since the illness as proof that she was a lousy coper. What troubled her most was not simply that she had changed, but that she no longer trusted her own capacity to handle what life might require.

By the time she sought help, Malia was exhausted by the narrowness of the world she had carved out for herself. She came because she was tired of waking at night to check for danger, tired of feeling her body react before her mind could catch up, and tired of letting smells, breathlessness, and medical surroundings dictate where she could go. She said she wanted to be able to breathe, sleep, and work without bracing for the next reminder of the illness. More than anything, she hoped for a way to feel safe again without needing her life to stay so small.
